questions.question: What are classes and objects in Ruby?
questions.title: Classes and Objects
questions.direct_answer: A Ruby **class** defines behaviour and the shape of an object's state; an **object** is one instance of that class. Calling `Book.new(...)` creates an object and normally runs its `initialize` method. Instance variables such as `@title` belong to that object, while instance methods operate with that object as `self`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a class is a blueprint, an object is an instance, new calls initialize, and @vars hold state.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to set @vars in initialize (nil later), or confusing class (Dog) with instance (d).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Class = blueprint; object = instance (Dog.new). new calls initialize; @vars = per-object state. Everything is an object. Inheritance: Puppy < Dog.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A class defines shared behaviour; an object is one instance of it.
- `.new` creates an instance and normally invokes `initialize`.
- Instance variables such as `@name` store per-object state.
- Instance methods run with the receiving object as `self`.
- Encapsulate state behind meaningful methods instead of exposing every field.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A class defines the shared behaviour for a kind of object. An object is one instance of that class, with its own state. Two `Book` objects use the methods defined by `Book`, but each object keeps a different `@title`.

Calling `Book.new("Clean Code")` creates a `Book` object and normally runs `initialize`. The initializer stores the starting state. Later, `book.label` sends the `label` message to that object, and `self` inside the method refers to `book`.

In this complete example, both objects share the same `label` method while their `@title` values remain separate. `attr_reader` allows outside code to read the title without giving it unrestricted write access.

Public methods should describe what an object can do, not only expose its storage. A method such as `account.withdraw(20)` can validate the change and preserve the object's rules. A class method such as `Book.new` belongs to the class, while an instance method such as `label` needs a particular object.

support.title: Class and object have different jobs

items.label: Class
items.detail: Defines shared instance methods such as `label`.

items.label: Object
items.detail: Keeps one book's state, such as its own `@title`.

beats.spokenText: Calling `Book.new("Clean Code")` creates a `Book` object and normally runs `initialize`. The initializer stores the starting state. Later, `book.label` sends the `label` message to that object, and `self` inside the method refers to `book`.

beats.cue: Demonstrate shared methods and separate state
beats.spokenText: In this complete example, both objects share the same `label` method while their `@title` values remain separate. `attr_reader` allows outside code to read the title without giving it unrestricted write access.

support.title: Two Book objects, two titles
support.code:
class Book
  attr_reader :title

  def initialize(title)
    @title = title
  end

  def label
    "Book: #{@title}"
  end
end

first = Book.new("Clean Code")
second = Book.new("Refactoring")
puts first.label
puts second.label
support.caption: The method comes from the class; `@title` belongs to each object.

beats.spokenText: Public methods should describe what an object can do, not only expose its storage. A method such as `account.withdraw(20)` can validate the change and preserve the object's rules. A class method such as `Book.new` belongs to the class, while an instance method such as `label` needs a particular object.
beats.recallRule: The class owns shared behaviour, each object owns its state, and public methods form the boundary between them.

sections.title: Creation, state, and message dispatch
sections.content:
`Book.new` is a class-method call. The normal creation path allocates storage for a Book instance and invokes its private `initialize` method with the supplied arguments. `initialize` configures the new object's starting state; its own return value is not used as the result of `.new`, which returns the created object.

An instance variable is attached to one object, not declared once for the whole class. If `first` and `second` are different Book instances, assigning `first`'s `@title` does not change `second`. An unread instance variable evaluates as `nil`, which is convenient but can hide a missed initialization unless the constructor establishes required values.

A method call chooses behaviour through the receiver's class and ancestor chain. In `book.label`, `book` is the receiver and becomes `self` while the selected method runs. Local variables disappear with the method call; instance variables remain with the object.

The public surface should describe what the object can do, not merely expose storage. `account.withdraw(20)` can reject a negative balance, log the operation, and preserve an invariant. Letting callers write `account.balance = -20` would make all of those rules optional.

sections.title: From class definition to one object
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Book class: methods] -->|Book.new title| A[allocate Book object]
  A -->|initialize title| O[object with @title]
  O -->|book.label| M[label runs with book as self]
  M --> R[returned label]
```

sections.title: Two objects share methods, not state
sections.content:
```ruby
class Book
  attr_reader :title

  def initialize(title)
    @title = title
  end

  def label
    "Book: #{@title}"
  end
end

first = Book.new('Clean Code')
second = Book.new('Refactoring')

first.label                 # => 'Book: Clean Code'
second.label                # => 'Book: Refactoring'
first.class                 # => Book
Book.class                  # => Class
```
